newsitem.title: USA: KOREAN AIR MET U.S. INSURANCE LIABILITY STANDARD.
newsitem.headline: KOREAN AIR MET U.S. INSURANCE LIABILITY STANDARD.

text.p: Korean Air Lines Co had enough liability insurance coverage to meet the U.S. government's minimum requirement for foreign carriers with operations in the United States, according to a U.S. government document.
The insurance certificate, filed with the U.S. Department of Transportation, showed that Korean Air Lines carried passenger bodily injury liability coverage of at least $300,000 per person.
The coverage, provided by Oriental Fire & Marine Insurance Co Ltd in Seoul, South Korea, took effect November 1, 1994.

On an occurence basis, the passenger bodily injury liability coverage was at least $300,000 multiplied by 75 percent of the total number of passenger seats installed in the aircraft, according to the foreign air carriers certificate of insurance.
Korean Air's Boeing 747-300 jumbo jets, like the one that crashed in Guam on Tuesday, usually seat about 430 passengers, according to industry statistics.
Korean Air Flight 801 was carrying 254 passengers and crew, including 231 passengers and 23 crew, when it crashed on Tuesday.

Most of the passengers were South Korean honeymooners, but 21 were foreigners, including 14 Americans, one Japanese and a New Zealander, as well as five unidentified foreign transiting passengers, officials in Seoul said.
About 200 people died in the crash, but the total number of survivors was still not clear.
It also was not clear whether the Warsaw Convention's limitation on compensation payments to victims and their families was still in effect.

The airline industry has been moving toward abandoning the limits set down under the 1929 Warsaw Convention, which are widely seen as too low and outdated, and accepting unlimited liability under a new International Air Transport Association (IATA) accord.
An aviation insurance lawyer familiar with the situation said he believed the new IATA accord was scheduled to go into effect on August 15.
The accord has been signed by more than 80 airlines representing 80 percent of scheduled international air traffic and including all big global carriers.
But, it also was not clear whether Korean Air had signed on to the agreement.
"The question is whether the new IATA agreement applies," the attorney said.
In addition, he said, the Guam airport authority may have some liability in this case and he said there would be no limit to the authority's liability.
However, Washington, D.C.-based airline industry attorney Mark Dombroff, said the Warsaw Convention's limits were still in effect.
Under the Warsaw Convention limits, an airline's liability is limited unless there is a finding of willful misconduct.
That, he said, is what happened with a Korean Air Lines 747 that was shot down by a Soviet fighter after flying through Soviet airspace near Sakhalin Island.
All 269 aboard were killed.
The amount of liability insurance carried by an airline, he said, is irrelevant, as airlines buy more insurance than they may ever need in order to protect the assets of the company.
